<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

  /* Reading mode hides the chrome and the empty .arxiv-html-header marker: the pinned JS reads
     the marker's display to know which way to toggle. The marker draws no box. */
  .arxiv-html-header { display: contents; }
  html[data-reading-mode="enabled"] :is(.arxiv-html-site-chrome, .arxiv-html-header, .ds-site-footer) { display: none; }
  /* The paper controls' icons are blocks, so they sit centred (the pinned JS shows the theme
     icon by making its span a block). */
  .arxiv-html-site-chrome .ds-site-header-tools svg { display: block; width: 18px; height: 18px; flex-shrink: 0; fill: currentColor; }
  /* ar5iv dims every image in dark mode and puts it on a white wash, for paper figures;
     arXiv's own render as they are (the logo on the bar, the funder logos on their white
     chips). Important: ar5iv's dark rules are unlayered, as specific as
     :root:not([data-theme]) img:not(.ltx_no_dark_filter). */
  :is(.ds-site-header, .ds-site-footer) img { filter: none !important; }
  .ds-site-header img { background-color: transparent !important; }

  /* Wide (the theme's 1280px): the theme lays the body out as a grid whose full-width top rows
     were the band's and its sticky reader bar's. The band takes the first and scrolls away; the
     header, the paper's bar (no site navigation, the paper's controls), takes the second and
     stays in view, the one sticky bar, with the anchor clearance that requires (DESIGN-POLICIES).
     The controls show their names. */
  @media (min-width: 1280px) {
    html { scroll-padding-top: 80px; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome { display: contents; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > #ds-announcement { grid-area: announce; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > .ds-site-header { grid-area: header; position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 3; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-icon { display: none; }
  }
  /* Narrow: the header scrolls away, and the controls show icons (names kept for screen
     readers; Why HTML? goes). The theme's contents panel is fixed below where its old sticky
     bar was, and hidden only once the reader has closed it, so until then it is an invisible box
     over the header and the paper: it shows only while open, under the chrome, in its place in
     the page. The paper's footer (build logs, reporting instructions) keeps the text's side
     inset; the theme gives it none, so it met the screen edges. */
  @media (max-width: 1279px) {
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-wide { display: none; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-label { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); white-space: nowrap; }
    html:not([data-toc-display="block"]) .ltx_page_navbar { display: none; }
    .ltx_page_navbar { position: absolute; top: auto; }
    .arxiv-html-footer { padding-inline: 1rem; }
  }

<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_section"><a href="#S5" title="In Surgical Refusal Ablation: Disentangling Safety from Intelligence via Concept-Guided Spectral Cleaning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">5 </span>Results</span></a>
<ol class="ltx_toclist ltx_toclist_section">

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_document">Surgical Refusal Ablation: Disentangling Safety from Intelligence via Concept-Guided Spectral Cleaning</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Tony Cristofano
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Email: </span><a href="mailto:"><span id="id1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">tcristo@gmail.com</span></a>
</span></span></span></span></div>
<div class="ltx_dates">January 2026</div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Safety-aligned instruction-tuned language models exhibit systematic refusal of harmful requests. While recent representation engineering work demonstrates that refusal can be modulated through low-dimensional activation steering, directly ablating the “refusal vector”—computed from contrastive harmful vs. harmless prompts—frequently induces collateral damage to model behavior and distribution drift.</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.2" class="ltx_p">We argue that this degradation occurs because the raw refusal vector is <span id="abstract1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">polysemantic</span>: it entangles the refusal signal with unrelated linguistic structure (syntax, formatting) and core capability circuits (math, coding, reasoning). We introduce <span id="abstract1.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Surgical Refusal Ablation (SRA)</span>, a technique for distilling steering directions before intervention. SRA constructs a registry of independent <span id="abstract1.2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Concept Atoms</span> representing protected capabilities and stylistic confounds, and uses <span id="abstract1.2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ridge-regularized spectral residualization</span> to orthogonalize the refusal vector against these directions. This yields a <span id="abstract1.2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">clean refusal direction</span> that targets refusal-relevant structure while minimizing disruption to the model’s semantic geometry.</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.3" class="ltx_p">Across five models (Qwen3-VL-2B/4B/8B, Ministral-3B/14B), SRA achieves deep refusal reduction (0–2% on our harmful suite) with negligible perplexity impact on <span id="abstract1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">wikitext_2_raw</span> (mean <math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta</annotation></semantics></math>PPL <math id="abstract1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≈</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx</annotation></semantics></math> +0.02) and minimal measured distribution drift (mean first-token KL <math id="abstract1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≈</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx</annotation></semantics></math> 0.025). Notably, on Qwen3-VL-4B, standard ablation induces severe distribution drift (KL = 2.088), whereas SRA maintains the original distribution (KL = 0.044) while achieving the same 0% refusal rate.</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.4" class="ltx_p">To evaluate capability retention at higher resolution than discrete task accuracy, we report teacher-forced perplexity on 1,000-example subsets from GSM8K (math) and MBPP (code). SRA preserves (and often improves) math/code perplexity across all five models (largest GSM8K increase: +0.0439), consistent with minimal capability-distribution disruption under this proxy. We use this framework to show that what appears to be “model damage” is often “Ghost Noise”—spectral bleeding of the dirty refusal direction into capability subspaces.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Modern instruction-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) integrate safety alignment through fine-tuning or preference optimization. A common emergent behavior is <span id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">refusal</span>—a stereotyped response to unsafe prompts. Recent work has shown that refusal can be mediated by a low-dimensional steering direction in activations, enabling ablation techniques that remove these directions to restore compliance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">However, a critical methodological limitation persists: <span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">the “refusal vector” is dirty.</span>
Commonly calculated by subtracting mean activations of harmless prompts from harmful ones, this direction captures not only refusal signals, but also syntactic structure, distributional shifts, and task-specific features.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We demonstrate that ablating this raw vector causes <span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">“Ghost Noise” damage</span>: spectral perturbations that erode critical capabilities like logic and coding. For example, in Qwen3-VL-2B we observe that the raw refusal direction exhibits non-trivial cosine similarity with protected capability atoms such as <span id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Logic</span> (approximately <math id="S1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-0.22" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.22</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-0.22</annotation></semantics></math>) and <span id="S1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Coding</span> (approximately <math id="S1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+0.18" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>0.18</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+0.18</annotation></semantics></math>), indicating entanglement between refusal and capability/style subspaces.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">This phenomenon suggests that capability degradation observed after naive refusal-direction ablation may not be an inherent trade-off, but instead an artifact of imprecise interventions that inadvertently remove capability-relevant directions correlated with the harmful prompt set.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">To address this, we introduce <span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Surgical Refusal Ablation (SRA)</span>, a method for cleaning refusal directions. Our contribution is threefold:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We diagnose refusal ablation as a <span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">polysemantic interference problem</span>, identifying how reasoning circuits are often entangled in the refusal direction.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce a <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Concept Atom Registry</span> and <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Spectral Residualization</span> procedure to distill the refusal vector by removing protected capability/style components.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We show SRA dramatically reduces measured distribution drift compared to standard ablation while preserving math/code distributions under a high-resolution perplexity proxy.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<section id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">High-level pipeline.</h4>

<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">SRA (i) maps the geometry of refusal against a registry of interpretable semantic atoms, (ii) cleans the refusal direction by residualizing against Shield and Confound atoms, and (iii) applies targeted low-rank weight updates scaled by a semantic energy proxy to ablate the cleaned signal while preserving the model’s original topology.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Activation Steering &amp; Refusal</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al. [1]</a></cite> identified that refusal is mediated by a low-rank direction in the residual stream. This relates to Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite> and related activation engineering methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite>. These methods often assume the contrastive vector represents a single concept; our findings emphasize that such vectors can be polysemantic and benefit from explicit cleaning.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Concept Erasure &amp; Orthogonalization</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Work like LEACE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite> and INLP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite> removes information from representations to prevent probing of specific attributes. SRA adapts this intuition to <span id="S2.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">behavioral circuits</span>: we do not want to erase “Logic”; we want to edit refusal while enforcing that the edit direction is orthogonal to protected capability/style directions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Weight Editing vs. Vector Quality</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Methods like ROME <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite>, MEMIT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>, and AlphaEdit <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite> edit parameters while constraining collateral damage. SRA is complementary: even with simple projection-style interventions, the limiting factor can be the <span id="S2.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">semantic purity of the vector being removed</span>. Cleaning the steering direction itself can substantially reduce side effects.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.4 </span>Model Editing</h3>

<div id="S2.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Targeted weight editing methods like MEND <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite> and instruction-based/localized edits like InstructEdit <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite> and GRACE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite> explore reliable updates with minimal collateral effects. Our work adapts low-rank projection updates to behavioral refusal subspaces rather than factual knowledge.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.5 </span>Null-Space Projection in Editing (Brief Connection)</h3>

<div id="S2.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our findings align with and extend the “orthogonality principle” formalized in AlphaEdit <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>. AlphaEdit shows that factual edits should be projected onto the null space of preserved knowledge keys to prevent forgetting. Here we show that behavioral edits benefit from projecting the intervention direction onto the null space of protected capability/style directions (Shields/Confounds), reducing capability drift.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Method: Surgical Refusal Ablation</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>The Polysemantic “Dirty” Vector</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{\ell}(\mathcal{D})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{\ell}(\mathcal{D})</annotation></semantics></math> denote the mean residual stream activation at layer <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math>. The standard refusal direction is:</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{r}_{\ell}^{\text{dirty}}=\mu_{\ell}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{harm}})-\mu_{\ell}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}})" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐫</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mtext>dirty</mtext></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>harm</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>safe</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{r}_{\ell}^{\text{dirty}}=\mu_{\ell}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{harm}})-\mu_{\ell}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">We hypothesize that <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{r}_{\ell}^{\text{dirty}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐫</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mtext>dirty</mtext></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{r}_{\ell}^{\text{dirty}}</annotation></semantics></math> is polysemantic:</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{r}_{\ell}^{\text{dirty}}=\mathbf{s}_{\ell}+\sum_{k}\alpha_{k}\mathbf{a}_{\ell}^{(k)}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐫</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mtext>dirty</mtext></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐬</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.055em">+</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mi>k</mi></munder><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐚</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{r}_{\ell}^{\text{dirty}}=\mathbf{s}_{\ell}+\sum_{k}\alpha_{k}\mathbf{a}_{\ell}^{(k)}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{s}_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐬</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{s}_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> is the refusal signal of interest, and <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{a}^{(k)}_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐚</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{a}^{(k)}_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> are independent concept directions (math, coding, style) that correlate with harmful prompts.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>The Semantic Atom Registry</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We construct a registry of <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Concept Atoms</span> to define a protected semantic space:</p>
<ul id="S3.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Targets (Attractors):</span> concepts representing refusal-relevant semantics (e.g., privacy, deception, epistemic uncertainty).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Shields (Constraints):</span> critical capabilities entangled with refusal (e.g., <span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Logic, Math, Coding, Curiosity</span>).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Confounds (Style):</span> stylistic/linguistic features correlated with refusal templates (e.g., <span id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">imperative negation grammar, sentiment, affirmatives</span>).</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Each atom is computed from a small contrastive pair of datasets:</p>
<table id="S3.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{a}^{(k)}_{\ell}=\mu_{\ell}(\mathcal{D}^{(k)}_{+})-\mu_{\ell}(\mathcal{D}^{(k)}_{-})" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐚</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{a}^{(k)}_{\ell}=\mu_{\ell}(\mathcal{D}^{(k)}_{+})-\mu_{\ell}(\mathcal{D}^{(k)}_{-})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Data-light construction.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In our implementation, each concept atom is computed from two short contrastive prompt files containing typically 10–15 prompts each (20–30 prompts total per atom). The harmful/harmless refusal contrast used to compute <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{r}_{\ell}^{\text{dirty}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐫</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mtext>dirty</mtext></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{r}_{\ell}^{\text{dirty}}</annotation></semantics></math> is larger (e.g., 112 harmful prompts with a matched harmless set). This separation is intentional: atoms are measured on independent datasets so they capture general capability/style directions rather than artifacts of the refusal prompt set.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Spectral Residualization (The Cleaning Step)</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We perform ridge-regularized regression of the dirty refusal vector on Shield+Confound atoms to estimate entangled components, then subtract them:</p>
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{w}}=\arg\min_{\mathbf{w}}\|\mathbf{r}_{\ell}^{\text{dirty}}-\mathbf{A}_{SC}\mathbf{w}\|^{2}+\lambda\|\mathbf{w}\|^{2}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐰</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><munder><mi>min</mi><mi>𝐰</mi></munder><mo>⁡</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐫</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mtext>dirty</mtext></msubsup><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐀</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐰</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>𝐰</mi><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{w}}=\arg\min_{\mathbf{w}}\|\mathbf{r}_{\ell}^{\text{dirty}}-\mathbf{A}_{SC}\mathbf{w}\|^{2}+\lambda\|\mathbf{w}\|^{2}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<table id="S3.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\mathbf{r}}_{\ell}=\mathbf{r}_{\ell}^{\text{dirty}}-\mathbf{A}_{SC}\hat{\mathbf{w}}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐫</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mtext>dirty</mtext></msubsup><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐀</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐰</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\mathbf{r}}_{\ell}=\mathbf{r}_{\ell}^{\text{dirty}}-\mathbf{A}_{SC}\hat{\mathbf{w}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{A}_{SC}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐀</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{A}_{SC}</annotation></semantics></math> is the matrix formed by concatenating Shield and Confound atoms. Intuitively, <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\mathbf{r}}_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\mathbf{r}}_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> removes the portion of the refusal direction that is predictable from protected capability/style directions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Iterative Hard-Negative Refinement</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We utilize an iterative loop where failed edits (prompts that still refuse) are fed back into the calculation to refine <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{r}_{\ell}^{\text{dirty}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐫</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mtext>dirty</mtext></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{r}_{\ell}^{\text{dirty}}</annotation></semantics></math>, ensuring the clean vector captures robust refusal modes.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.5 </span>Rank-One Weight Update</h3>

<div id="S3.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We apply a rank-one projection update to selected projection matrices (MLP and/or attention) to suppress the clean refusal direction. For a weight matrix <math id="S3.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐖</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}</annotation></semantics></math> and unit direction <math id="S3.SS5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐯</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}</annotation></semantics></math> aligned with <math id="S3.SS5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\mathbf{r}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\mathbf{r}}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}^{\prime}=(\mathbf{I}-\gamma\mathbf{v}\mathbf{v}^{\top})\mathbf{W}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>𝐈</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝐯𝐯</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}^{\prime}=(\mathbf{I}-\gamma\mathbf{v}\mathbf{v}^{\top})\mathbf{W}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS5.p1.2" class="ltx_p">This suppresses components aligned with <math id="S3.SS5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐯</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}</annotation></semantics></math> in the output space of the projection while leaving orthogonal components minimally perturbed.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Choosing <math id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> (Semantic Energy Proxy).</h4>

<div id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We scale edit strength using a <em id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Semantic Energy Proxy</em> to reflect refusal-relevant signal magnitude at layer <math id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math>. One simple choice is to set <math id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma_{\ell}\propto\|\mathbf{a}^{(\text{dec})}_{\ell}\|_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>γ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>∝</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐚</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>dec</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma_{\ell}\propto\|\mathbf{a}^{(\text{dec})}_{\ell}\|_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{a}^{(\text{dec})}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐚</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>dec</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{a}^{(\text{dec})}</annotation></semantics></math> is a representative Target atom such as <span id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Deception</span>. In practice, <math id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> can also be stabilized by calibrating to typical activation magnitudes at the edit site.</p>
</div>
<figure id="alg1" class="ltx_float ltx_float_algorithm ltx_framed ltx_framed_top">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_float"><span id="alg1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Algorithm 1</span> </span> Iterative Surgical Refusal Ablation (SRA)</figcaption>
<div id="alg1.4" class="ltx_listing ltx_framed ltx_framed_topbottom ltx_listing">
<div id="alg1.l0" class="ltx_listingline">
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l0.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">0:</span></span>
                
                
               Model <math id="alg1.l0.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>, harmful set <math id="alg1.l0.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\text{harm}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>harm</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\text{harm}}</annotation></semantics></math>, harmless set <math id="alg1.l0.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>safe</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}}</annotation></semantics></math>, concept registry datasets <math id="alg1.l0.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\mathcal{D}^{(k)}_{+},\mathcal{D}^{(k)}_{-}\}_{k=1}^{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\mathcal{D}^{(k)}_{+},\mathcal{D}^{(k)}_{-}\}_{k=1}^{K}</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>
<div id="alg1.l1" class="ltx_listingline">
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">1:</span></span>
                
                
               Choose target layers (e.g., 15–25) and target projection matrices.

</div>
<div id="alg1.l2" class="ltx_listingline">
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">2:</span></span>
                
                
               <span id="alg1.l2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span> <math id="alg1.l2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t=1</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="alg1.l2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="alg1.l2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">do</span>



</div>
<div id="alg1.l3" class="ltx_listingline">
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">3:</span></span>
                
                
                Compute dirty refusal direction <math id="alg1.l3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{r}^{\text{dirty}}_{\ell}=\mu_{\ell}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{harm}})-\mu_{\ell}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐫</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mtext>dirty</mtext></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>harm</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>safe</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{r}^{\text{dirty}}_{\ell}=\mu_{\ell}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{harm}})-\mu_{\ell}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}})</annotation></semantics></math>.

</div>
<div id="alg1.l4" class="ltx_listingline">
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">4:</span></span>
                
                
                Compute concept atoms <math id="alg1.l4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{a}^{(k)}_{\ell}=\mu_{\ell}(\mathcal{D}^{(k)}_{+})-\mu_{\ell}(\mathcal{D}^{(k)}_{-})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐚</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{a}^{(k)}_{\ell}=\mu_{\ell}(\mathcal{D}^{(k)}_{+})-\mu_{\ell}(\mathcal{D}^{(k)}_{-})</annotation></semantics></math>.

</div>
<div id="alg1.l5" class="ltx_listingline">
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">5:</span></span>
                
                
                Form <math id="alg1.l5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{A}_{SC}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐀</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{A}_{SC}</annotation></semantics></math> from Shield + Confound atoms.

</div>
<div id="alg1.l6" class="ltx_listingline">
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">6:</span></span>
                
                
                Residualize: <math id="alg1.l6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\mathbf{r}}_{\ell}\leftarrow\mathbf{r}^{\text{dirty}}_{\ell}-\mathbf{A}_{SC}\hat{\mathbf{w}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐫</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mtext>dirty</mtext></msubsup><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐀</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐰</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\mathbf{r}}_{\ell}\leftarrow\mathbf{r}^{\text{dirty}}_{\ell}-\mathbf{A}_{SC}\hat{\mathbf{w}}</annotation></semantics></math> (ridge regression).

</div>
<div id="alg1.l7" class="ltx_listingline">
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l7.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">7:</span></span>
                
                
                Apply rank-one update(s): <math id="alg1.l7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}\leftarrow(\mathbf{I}-\gamma\mathbf{v}\mathbf{v}^{\top})\mathbf{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>𝐈</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝐯𝐯</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}\leftarrow(\mathbf{I}-\gamma\mathbf{v}\mathbf{v}^{\top})\mathbf{W}</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="alg1.l7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}=\tilde{\mathbf{r}}/\|\tilde{\mathbf{r}}\|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐯</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}=\tilde{\mathbf{r}}/\|\tilde{\mathbf{r}}\|</annotation></semantics></math>.

</div>
<div id="alg1.l8" class="ltx_listingline">
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l8.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">8:</span></span>
                
                
                Mine hard negatives: update <math id="alg1.l8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\text{harm}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>harm</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\text{harm}}</annotation></semantics></math> to prompts still refused by <math id="alg1.l8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>.

</div>
<div id="alg1.l9" class="ltx_listingline">
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l9.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">9:</span></span>
                
                
               <span id="alg1.l9.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">end</span> <span id="alg1.l9.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span>
</div>
</div>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Empirical Evidence: The Anatomy of a Dirty Vector</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Concept Orthogonality Map</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We measure cosine similarity among concept atoms and the refusal vectors across layers 15–25. The map reveals that the dirty refusal vector exhibits non-trivial correlations with multiple capability/style directions, indicating polysemantic entanglement.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2601.08489v1/Figure1.png" id="S4.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/362;" width="452" height="362" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S4.F1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Heatmap across concept atoms and the dirty refusal vector.<span id="S4.F1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> The dirty vector correlates with multiple semantic/style components, motivating cleaning via residualization.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Spectral Breakdown: The Anatomy of a “Dirty” Vector</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We compare the projection magnitude of the Standard (dirty) vector vs. the Surgical (cleaned) vector on representative Targets, Shields, and Style confounds. Standard ablation suppresses Shields (e.g., coding/logic/math) nearly as strongly as refusal-related Targets, while SRA preserves Shields by removing their components from the intervention direction.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2601.08489v1/Figure2.png" id="S4.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:467/234;" width="467" height="234" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S4.F2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Spectral Breakdown: The Anatomy of a “Dirty” Vector.<span id="S4.F2.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Standard (dirty) and Surgical (cleaned) vectors projected onto concept atoms. SRA removes “Ghost Noise” components aligned with Shield/Style directions while retaining Target (refusal-relevant) signal.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Evolution of Semantic Components During Surgery</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">During iterative refinement, Target projections decrease rapidly while Shield projections remain near baseline. This motivates a practical stop condition: stop once Target signal collapses (further edits yield diminishing returns and risk over-editing).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2601.08489v1/Figure3.png" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/283;" width="452" height="283" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S4.F3.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Evolution of Semantic Components During Surgery (example: Qwen3-VL-2B, Layer 25).<span id="S4.F3.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Target components diminish across passes while Shield components remain comparatively stable, indicating targeted removal.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Results</h2>

<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Evaluation Setup (Refusal, Drift, and Capability)</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We report three evaluation axes:</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Refusal rate (Table <a href="#S5.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 5.2 Distribution Drift and Refusal Reduction (Multi-Model) ‣ 5 Results ‣ Surgical Refusal Ablation: Disentangling Safety from Intelligence via Concept-Guided Spectral Cleaning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>).</h4>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Refusal is measured on a harmful prompt suite (e.g., 112 harmful prompts, with a matched harmless set when needed for contrastive construction) using an automated rubric and reported as a binary outcome (<em id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">refusal</em> vs. <em id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">responded</em>). A response is counted as a <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">hard refusal</span> if it explicitly declines (e.g., “I can’t help with that”). A <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">soft refusal</span> includes deflection or non-answers. We also treat <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">hedging that requires a follow-up</span> as a failure. Responses that include <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">warnings</span> are <em id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.7" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">not</em> counted as refusals so long as they provide the information.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Distribution drift (Table <a href="#S5.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 5.2 Distribution Drift and Refusal Reduction (Multi-Model) ‣ 5 Results ‣ Surgical Refusal Ablation: Disentangling Safety from Intelligence via Concept-Guided Spectral Cleaning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>).</h4>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Distribution drift is measured on the standard <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">wikitext_2_raw</span> dataset. Perplexity (PPL) is computed with standard <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">teacher-forced</span> next-token evaluation over the <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">full sequence</span>. KL divergence is computed as a <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">single-step, first-token</span> measure: for each evaluation context <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>, we compute <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathrm{KL}\!\left(p_{\text{edit}}(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,p_{\text{base}}(\cdot\mid x)\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mpadded style="width:1.431em;" width="1.431em"><mi>KL</mi></mpadded><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>edit</mtext></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0.337em">∥</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>base</mtext></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{KL}\!\left(p_{\text{edit}}(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,p_{\text{base}}(\cdot\mid x)\right)</annotation></semantics></math> using the next-token distributions at the first generated token, then average across contexts.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Capability retention via perplexity (Table <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 5.5 Capability Retention (Math &amp; Code) via Perplexity ‣ 5 Results ‣ Surgical Refusal Ablation: Disentangling Safety from Intelligence via Concept-Guided Spectral Cleaning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).</h4>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While prior work in model editing (e.g., AlphaEdit) typically evaluates capability retention via downstream task accuracy (e.g., GLUE) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>, accuracy is often a blunt instrument that masks “Ghost Noise” and distributional rot until a threshold of catastrophic collapse is reached. In this work, we employ <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Teacher-Forced Perplexity (PPL)</span> as a high-resolution proxy for capability retention.
Concretely, we compute teacher-forced, full-sequence perplexity on subsets of 1,000 examples each from the GSM8K (math) and MBPP (code) standard test sets (Seed: 42).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Distribution Drift and Refusal Reduction (Multi-Model)</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate refusal reduction alongside distribution drift on standard text using perplexity (PPL), <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta</annotation></semantics></math>PPL, and first-token KL divergence. Standard ablation often induces large drift; SRA achieves comparable or stronger refusal reduction with minimal drift.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T1" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S5.T1.3" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<thead class="ltx_thead">
<tr id="S5.T1.3.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S5.T1.3.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt"><span id="S5.T1.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Model</span></th>
<th id="S5.T1.3.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt"><span id="S5.T1.3.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Method</span></th>
<th id="S5.T1.3.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt"><span id="S5.T1.3.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Refusal% <math id="S5.T1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\downarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↓</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\downarrow</annotation></semantics></math></span></th>

<th id="S5.T1.3.1.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt"><span id="S5.T1.3.1.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">KL</span></th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="S5.T1.3.2" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S5.T1.3.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_t" rowspan="3"><span id="S5.T1.3.2.1.1" class="ltx_text">Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct</span></th>
<th id="S5.T1.3.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_t">Base</th>
<td id="S5.T1.3.2.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">83.3%</td>

<td id="S5.T1.3.2.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">0.000</td>
<td id="S5.T1.3.2.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">0.000</td></tr>
<tr id="S5.T1.3.3" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S5.T1.3.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row">Standard</th>
<td id="S5.T1.3.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center">0.0%</td>
<td id="S5.T1.3.3.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center">8.834</td>
<td id="S5.T1.3.3.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center">+1.568</td>

<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>Analysis of Distribution Drift (KL)</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The most striking proxy result is first-token KL divergence:</p>
<ul id="S5.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S5.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Qwen3-VL-4B:</span> Standard ablation induces a massive distribution shift (KL = 2.088), whereas SRA reduces drift to KL = 0.044 (approximately a 47<math id="S5.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> reduction) while achieving the same 0% refusal rate.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Qwen3-VL-2B:</span> SRA yields a 34<math id="S5.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> reduction in KL drift (0.622 vs. 0.018) and a 56<math id="S5.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> reduction in PPL damage (<math id="S5.I1.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta</annotation></semantics></math>PPL +1.568 vs. +0.028) relative to standard ablation.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">These results support the hypothesis that much of the observed “damage” under standard ablation reflects distributional warping induced by removing syntactic/style/capability components entangled in the dirty refusal direction.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.4 </span>Spectral Dynamics: The Anatomy of Collapse</h3>

<div id="S5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We analyze the evolution of the refusal direction across multiple SRA passes on Qwen3-VL-2B (Layer 25). The spectral decomposition (Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.3 Evolution of Semantic Components During Surgery ‣ 4 Empirical Evidence: The Anatomy of a Dirty Vector ‣ Surgical Refusal Ablation: Disentangling Safety from Intelligence via Concept-Guided Spectral Cleaning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>) reveals a distinct “peeling” of refusal mechanisms:</p>
<ul id="S5.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S5.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S5.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Pass 1 (The Blockade):</span> The vector is dominated by <span id="S5.I2.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Deception</span> (coefficient <math id="S5.I2.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx 6.42" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mn>6.42</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 6.42</annotation></semantics></math>) and <span id="S5.I2.i1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Privacy</span> (coefficient <math id="S5.I2.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx 2.95" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mn>2.95</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 2.95</annotation></semantics></math>). Refusal primarily manifests as simulating policy constraints.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S5.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Pass 2–3 (The Retreat):</span> As deception-like structure is ablated, the vector rotates. By Pass 3, the <span id="S5.I2.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Deception</span> component collapses (<math id="S5.I2.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx 0.40" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mn>0.40</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 0.40</annotation></semantics></math>), but <span id="S5.I2.i2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Epistemic Uncertainty</span> remains dominant (<math id="S5.I2.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx 2.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mn>2.01</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 2.01</annotation></semantics></math>). The model shifts from “I cannot allow this” to “I do not know this.”</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S5.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I2.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Pass 4 (Signal Collapse):</span> Refusal structure dissolves. The explained variance (<math id="S5.I2.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>) of the atom-regression fit drops from <math id="S5.I2.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx 3.5\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mn>3.5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 3.5\%</annotation></semantics></math> (Pass 1) to <math id="S5.I2.i3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx 0.4\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mn>0.4</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 0.4\%</annotation></semantics></math> (Pass 4), indicating that the remaining residual no longer aligns with the interpretable atom registry.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.5 </span>Capability Retention (Math &amp; Code) via Perplexity</h3>

<div id="S5.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We report teacher-forced, full-sequence perplexity on 1,000-example subsets from GSM8K (math) and MBPP (code) test sets (Seed: 42). Lower perplexity indicates better next-token predictive fit on these domain-specific distributions.</p>
</div>

<tr id="S5.T2.3.3" class="ltx_tr">

<td id="S5.T2.3.3.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t"><span id="S5.T2.3.3.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">9.2615</span></td>
<td id="S5.T2.3.3.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t"><span id="S5.T2.3.3.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">9.0212</span></td>
<td id="S5.T2.3.3.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t"><span id="S5.T2.3.3.7.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">-0.2403</span></td></tr>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2: </span>Capability retention measured via teacher-forced, full-sequence perplexity on 1,000-example subsets from GSM8K and MBPP test sets (Seed: 42). <math id="S5.T2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta</annotation></semantics></math> is computed as (SRA <math id="S5.T2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>−</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-</annotation></semantics></math> Base).</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Across all evaluated models, SRA does not increase perplexity on MBPP and produces only minor changes on GSM8K (largest increase: +0.0439 on Qwen3-VL-2B), suggesting no evidence of broad capability-distribution degradation under this high-resolution proxy.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Discussion</h2>

<section id="S6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.1 </span>The Mechanism of “Ghost Noise” Damage</h3>

<div id="S6.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Why does a simple vector ablation cause broad capability loss? Our results suggest the dirty refusal vector shares spectral structure with many capability/style circuits. Removing it suppresses generic linguistic machinery (e.g., negation/imperative grammar) and reasoning components (e.g., coding/math) that are not inherently “refusal,” producing perplexity spikes and distribution drift.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.2 </span>The Scaling Hypothesis</h3>

<div id="S6.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A notable finding is that Standard Ablation fails to fully uncensor larger models (e.g., Qwen3-VL-8B, Ministral-14B) compared to smaller ones. One interpretation is that as models scale, refusal becomes increasingly abstract/semantic rather than surface-template driven. In that regime, a single dirty contrastive direction may capture mostly stylistic/lexical artifacts while missing deeper refusal circuitry. Concept-guided triangulation (Targets like epistemic/deception/privacy) helps intersect the deeper circuit.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.3 </span>The “Orthogonality Principle” of Model Editing</h3>

<div id="S6.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our findings align with and extend AlphaEdit <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>: interference is reduced when an edit direction is orthogonal to protected competencies. AlphaEdit applies this to knowledge keys; we apply it to capability/style atoms. This suggests a unified rule: <em id="S6.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">edits are safest when projected away from the subspace representing core model competencies.</em></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.4 </span>Implications for the “Safety Tax”</h3>

<div id="S6.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">It is often assumed safety alignment imposes an inevitable “alignment tax”—a reduction in model capability. Our results challenge that framing: the near-zero drift and stable math/code perplexity under SRA suggest refusal-related behavior can be edited with minimal collateral damage when the intervention is sufficiently precise. Much of the “tax” observed in prior ablations may be attributable to dirty vectors and imprecise interventions.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Limitations</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our atom registry is curated and may miss confounds; unseen entanglers could still leak into the refusal direction. Automating atom discovery (or expanding registries) is a promising direction. Additionally, we do not claim SRA is a safety method; it is a behavioral editing tool. We also note evaluation limitations: (i) refusal detection remains definition-dependent; (ii) our harmful prompt suites are finite; and (iii) proxy drift metrics (PPL and first-token KL) do not substitute for comprehensive downstream behavioral evaluation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S8" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">8 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce Surgical Refusal Ablation (SRA), treating refusal ablation as a semantic disentanglement problem. By cleaning the steering vector of capability/style confounds and applying a low-rank intervention, we achieve behavioral editing with dramatically reduced measured distribution drift and preserved math/code distributions under a high-resolution perplexity proxy, compared to standard ablation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Appendix A: Theoretical Analysis — Capability Preservation via Null Space Projection</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Here we provide a formal justification for why SRA prevents capability damage and reduces distribution drift. This appendix mirrors the high-level orthogonality argument used in protected-editing work (e.g., AlphaEdit <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>), but instantiates the protected subspace using compact, interpretable Shield/Confound atoms rather than corpus-scale preserved keys.</p>
</div>
<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Problem Formulation</h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{ref}}(\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>ref</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{ref}}(\theta)</annotation></semantics></math> be the loss associated with refusal behavior and <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{cap}}(\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>cap</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{cap}}(\theta)</annotation></semantics></math> be a loss associated with general capabilities (e.g., next-token prediction). A naive ablation updates parameters in direction <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐯</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="A1.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta^{\prime}=\theta-\gamma\mathbf{v}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐯</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta^{\prime}=\theta-\gamma\mathbf{v}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</section>

<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>First-Order Condition for “Lossless” Editing</h3>

<div id="A1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We approximate the change in capability loss using a first-order Taylor expansion:</p>

<p id="A1.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Thus, to minimize capability drift, the intervention direction <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐯</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}</annotation></semantics></math> should be orthogonal to the gradient of capability loss:</p>

<section id="A1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.3 </span>The “Dirty” Vector Assumption</h3>

<div id="A1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Standard methods use <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}\propto\mathbf{r}_{\text{dirty}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐯</mi><mo>∝</mo><msub><mi>𝐫</mi><mtext>dirty</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}\propto\mathbf{r}_{\text{dirty}}</annotation></semantics></math>. Empirically, <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{r}_{\text{dirty}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐫</mi><mtext>dirty</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{r}_{\text{dirty}}</annotation></semantics></math> has non-zero cosine similarity with Shield atoms. If the dominant components of <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{cap}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>θ</mi></msub><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>cap</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{cap}}</annotation></semantics></math> lie primarily in the Shield span (denote it <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{A}_{\text{shield}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐀</mi><mtext>shield</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{A}_{\text{shield}}</annotation></semantics></math>), then:</p>
<table id="A1.E10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\langle\mathbf{r}_{\text{dirty}},\mathbf{A}_{\text{shield}}\rangle\neq 0" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐫</mi><mtext>dirty</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐀</mi><mtext>shield</mtext></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\langle\mathbf{r}_{\text{dirty}},\mathbf{A}_{\text{shield}}\rangle\neq 0</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
